with modified rows
instead supplies
its complete
boundary comparison
and its own gap
proof. A collar
can make those
differences small
at the rows
that are used;
it does not
erase them
as identities.

\subsubsection{The site readout at an outward row}

The site average used in the
Landau projector has one value
at each top, taken at that
top's assigned level. The
endpoint readout of a row
is a different list when
the row is outward.
We now give their exact
relation.

Let \(\mathsf T_j(y,x)\)
be the product of the
admitted internal mean
transports from a level-\(j\)
center \(y\) down its
pillar to a bare site \(x\).
For a top of level \(j\)
define
\begin{equation}
 (Q'_{\rm pill}\lambda)(y)
   =L^{-4j}\sum_{x\in B^j(y)}
                 \operatorname{Ad}(\mathsf T_j(y,x))\lambda(x).
 \label{px:own-pillar-site-average}
\end{equation}
These pillars are disjoint.
There is therefore an explicit
right inverse on node fields:
\begin{equation}
 (E_{\rm pill}\psi)(x)
      =\operatorname{Ad}(\mathsf T_j(y,x))^{-1}\psi(y)
       \quad (x\in B^j(y)),\qquad
                 Q'_{\rm pill}E_{\rm pill}=1 .
 \label{px:site-right-inverse}
\end{equation}
This proves rank without
an elliptic estimate.
For real transports the
right inverse has
supremum norm one.
With fine site measure
\(\eta^4\) and top
measure \(\xi_y^4\),
it is also an
isometry in \(L^2\).
Indeed a pillar
contains \(L^{4j}\)
bare sites, so
\(\eta^4L^{4j}=\xi_y^4\).
The invariant bilinear
color pairing gives
\begin{equation}
 Q'_{\rm pill}=E_{\rm pill}^\sharp,\qquad
                  Q'_{\rm pill}(Q'_{\rm pill})^\sharp=1.
 \label{px:site-weighted-adjoint}
\end{equation}
The algebraic identities
hold for admitted complex
transports as well.
Their Hermitian norm
bounds then include
the actual condition
numbers of those
transports.
A counting kernel
must include the
ratio \(\xi_y^4/\eta^4\)
in the transpose;
an ordinary
unweighted array
transpose would
not be \eqref{px:site-weighted-adjoint}.

For any level-\(j\) center
\(z\), write \(Q'_j\lambda(z)\)
for its full \(j\)-fold
transported site average,
whether or not its assigned
top level is \(j\).
If \(z\) is the outer
endpoint of a determining
level-\(j\) row, its
assigned level is \(j-1\).
The entire block \(B^j(z)\)
lies in that outer
layer. Decompose it
into its \(L^4\)
level-\((j-1)\)
pillars. The product
definition of the
transport gives
\begin{equation}
 Q'_j\lambda(z)
     =L^{-4}\sum_{w\in B(z)\cap\mathbb T^{(j-1)}}
        \operatorname{Ad}(T_{z,w}(\mathcal M^{j-1}U))
                               (Q'_{\rm pill}\lambda)(w).
 \label{px:outward-site-extension}
\end{equation}
To verify the coefficient,
each smaller average has
weight \(L^{-4(j-1)}\);
multiplying it by
\(L^{-4}\) gives
\(L^{-4j}\).
The two transport
factors multiply
in their path order.
This proves \eqref{px:outward-site-extension}
exactly, without
an asymptotic
or small-field
approximation.

Define \(\mathcal E_{j,z}\psi\)
to be \(\psi(z)\) at an
assigned level-\(j\) top,
and to be the finite
average on the right
of \eqref{px:outward-site-extension} at an
outer endpoint.
Then define the extended
coarse difference by
\begin{equation}
 (\bar D_{\rm ext}\psi)(c)
   =\xi_c^{-1}\{
          \mathcal E_{j,c_-}\psi
               -\operatorname{Ad}((\mathcal M^jU)(c))
                          \mathcal E_{j,c_+}\psi\},
                         \qquad c\in\Gamma_j .
 \label{px:extended-coarse-difference}
\end{equation}
For an interior row it
is the ordinary covariant
difference of its two
top values. For an
outward row it
first averages the
outer finer tops.
There is no need
to duplicate that
site as a new
independent top
in the site Gram
matrix.

Here is a direct verification
of the field intertwining.
Under an infinitesimal
gauge \(e^{it\lambda}\)
the derivative of the
level-\(j\) node factor
is
\begin{equation}
 \left.\frac1i\frac d{dt}v_j[tD_U^{\rm phys}\lambda](y)\right|_{t=0}
                         =\lambda(y)-Q'_j\lambda(y).
 \label{px:node-factor-gauge-derivative}
\end{equation}
At one step the change in
each relative contour has
derivative
\(\lambda(y)-\operatorname{Ad}(T_{y,x})\lambda(x)\).
The implicit mean at the
identity has differential
the arithmetic mean of
its inputs, so this
gives the one-step
formula. Iterating
and using the product
rule for the
accumulated node
factors gives
\eqref{px:node-factor-gauge-derivative}, with the
hierarchical site
average in \eqref{px:own-pillar-site-average}.

Differentiate the actual
straightening identity
\(\mathcal M^j(e^{i\eta A}U)
 =v_j[A]\,e^{iq_j^{\rm st}(A)}
          \mathcal M^jU\,v_j[A]^{-1}\)
on a row.
The plain coarse
variation is
\(\lambda(c_-)
-\operatorname{Ad}(\mathcal M^jU(c))\lambda(c_+)\).
Subtract the two
node derivatives
\eqref{px:node-factor-gauge-derivative}, with their
endpoint transports.
The remaining variation
is
\begin{equation}
 Dq_j^{\rm st}(0)\,D_U^{\rm phys}\lambda
     =Q'_j\lambda(c_-)
             -\operatorname{Ad}(\mathcal M^jU(c))Q'_j\lambda(c_+).
 \label{px:raw-straightened-intertwining}
\end{equation}
Divide by \(\xi_c\)
to obtain the
per-length row \(Q\).
Using \eqref{px:outward-site-extension} proves
the fully typed identity
\begin{equation}
                 QD_U^{\rm phys}
                          =\bar D_{\rm ext}Q'_{\rm pill}.
 \label{px:typed-seam-intertwining}
\end{equation}
This supplies the
intertwining needed
in \eqref{px:explicit-current-green}--\eqref{px:off-current-slice-defect}.
There \(\bar D\)
means this extended
row difference and
\(Q'\) means the
own-pillar site map.
Using a single
unextended value
of the outer
top would give
the wrong formula.

Each endpoint extension reads
at most \(L^4\) tops in
one adjacent layer.
Its real row sum is
at most one, since
the transports are
unitary and the
weights add to one.
A finer top occurs
in one such outer
block and at most
eight incident
coarse rows.
Thus its two-sided
normalized cell
counts are bounded
at fixed \(L\),
without a factor
depending on the
depth.
For complex pairs
the same statement
uses the actual
bounded transport
condition numbers.
The latter are
atomic domain
estimates; the
algebraic
intertwining does
not prove them.

\subsubsection{Finite real existence of the site operators}

There is also a real finite positivity
statement independent of a quantitative
inverse bound. Assume the actual
mean transports are admitted and
unitary, and that every active fine
site lies in a connected pillar
with its top. Let \(a\) be
strictly positive on the
top space. Then
\begin{equation}
 L_{\rm site}=D_U^\sharp D_U+
                    (Q'_{\rm pill})^\sharp aQ'_{\rm pill}
                         \quad\text{is strictly positive}.
 \label{px:finite-site-positivity}
\end{equation}
To prove it, a vector of zero
Hermitian energy must obey
\(D_U\lambda=0\) and
\(Q'_{\rm pill}\lambda=0\).
Split into Hermitian real
and imaginary parts;
it suffices to treat
real \(\lambda\).
The first identity means that
\(e^{it\lambda(x)}\) leaves
every active bond unchanged:
\begin{equation}
 e^{it\lambda(b_-)}U_b
                        e^{-it\lambda(b_+)}=U_b.
 \label{px:parallel-gauge-stabilizer}
\end{equation}
Gauge covariance of each actual
mean transport therefore gives
\(\operatorname{Ad}(\mathsf T_j(y,x))\lambda(x)
 =\lambda(y)\).
Average over the pillar:
\(Q'_{\rm pill}\lambda(y)=\lambda(y)\).
Its zero value makes
\(\lambda(y)=0\).
Parallel transport along
the active graph from
the top to every
site makes
\(\lambda=0\).
This proves \eqref{px:finite-site-positivity}.

It follows that \(G'=L_{\rm site}^{-1}\)
exists on every finite real
problem of this type.
The site Gram matrix
\begin{equation}
 Q'_{\rm pill}G'^2(Q'_{\rm pill})^\sharp
 \label{px:finite-site-gram}
\end{equation}
is strictly positive as well.
For a nonzero node vector
\(\psi\), surjectivity makes
\((Q'_{\rm pill})^\sharp\psi\ne0\);
invertibility of \(G'\)
then makes its squared
norm positive.
Thus the formulas for
\(R\) and \(\mathsf S\)
are genuine finite
real matrices before
their uniform bounds
are established.

No volume-uniform or scale-weighted
lower bound has been deduced
from this nullspace argument.
That bound needs the
quantitative site Poincaré
and local-gauge estimates.
Nor does \eqref{px:finite-site-positivity} prove
positivity of the fine
Wilson Hessian or
of its independent-current
completion.
The distinctions between
finite invertibility,
uniform coercivity and
exponentially local
readouts remain
necessary.

\subsubsection{Transport control on one pillar}

The site gap has a quantitative proof
from the actual averages. Let a
pillar have side \(\xi=n\eta\),
where \(n=L^j\), and assume
\begin{equation}
 |\partial U(p)-1|\le
                 \epsilon\,\eta^2\xi^{-2}
 \label{px:pillar-curvature}
\end{equation}
on its determining neighborhood.
The fixed path neighborhood has
an embedded rectangular lift.
If an extra fine collar is
needed, the regularity bounds
in the adjacent layer give
the same inequality with a
fixed \(L\)-dependent factor.
We include that factor in
the constants below.

Take the fine coordinate comb
from the pillar center and
put \(g(x)=U(\Gamma_{y,x})\).
For adjacent \(x,x+\eta e_\mu\),
the loop made by the two
root combs and that bond
is filled by strips of
width one fine cell.
Commuting the extra
\(\mu\)-step through
the later coordinate
segments uses at most
\(Cn\) plaquettes,
not \(Cn^2\).
The unitary Stokes
product inequality
therefore gives
\begin{equation}
 |U^g(b)-1|\le C\epsilon/n
                  \quad\text{on internal fine bonds}.
 \label{px:fine-comb-strip}
\end{equation}
Here \(g(y)=1\).
Every curvature norm is unchanged.
The gauge need not be
close to one, and its
derivatives are not
estimated in this step.

Write \(\xi_r=L^r\eta\),
and let \(a_r\) be the
supremum of
\(|\mathcal M^r(U^g)(c)-1|\)
on the level-\(r\)
internal edges used
in the hierarchical
transport. Let
\(\varpi_r\) be the
corresponding coarse
plaquette bound.
The determining
neighborhoods remain
in the rectangular
pillar neighborhood:
each parent block
is a union of
its child blocks,
and each contour
stays in its
assigned block.
The real curvature
iteration proved
in the background
section gives
\begin{equation}
 \varpi_r\le C_L\epsilon(\xi_r/\xi)^2 .
 \label{px:pillar-coarse-curvature}
\end{equation}
The same finite comparison
shows that one actual
averaged edge differs
from its central
straight transport
by at most
\(C_L\varpi_r\).
Indeed every closed
logarithm in its
definition is a
comparison loop
with that central
transport. The
unitary strip
estimate bounds
those logarithms,
and then their
exponential average.
The central route
has \(L\) edges,
so
\begin{equation}
       a_{r+1}\le L a_r+C_L\varpi_r .
 \label{px:pillar-open-recurrence}
\end{equation}
The coefficient of \(a_r\)
is exactly \(L\), by
the unitary product
inequality.

Iterating \eqref{px:pillar-open-recurrence}, using
\(a_0\le C\epsilon\eta/\xi\),
gives
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 a_r&\le L^ra_0+
       C_L\epsilon\sum_{s<r}
                 L^{r-1-s}(\xi_s/\xi)^2\\
     &\le C_L\epsilon\,\xi_r/\xi .
 \end{split}
 \label{px:pillar-open-bound}
\end{equation}
For the sum, insert
\(\xi_s=\eta L^s\);
its geometric factor is
bounded by a constant
times \((\xi_r/\xi)^2\),
which is no larger
than \(\xi_r/\xi\).
The constants do
not multiply with
the number of
levels.

The internal mean on
level \(r\) is a
finite smooth mean
of paths of \(O(L)\)
edges. On its
regular near-identity
chart it differs
from one by at
most \(C_La_r\).
The hierarchical
transport has one
such factor at
each level below
\(j\). All are
unitary, hence
\begin{equation}
 |\mathsf T_j(U^g;y,x)-1|
       \le C_L\sum_{r<j}a_r
       \le C_L\epsilon
                    \quad(x\in B^j(y)).
 \label{px:uniform-pillar-transport}
\end{equation}
The last sum uses
\(\sum_{r<j}\xi_r/\xi
  \le1/(L-1)\).
The fixed smallness
of \(\epsilon\)
also admits every
mean used in this
argument. Thus
\eqref{px:uniform-pillar-transport} is a
uniform-depth
property of
the actual
iterated transports,
not a hypothesis
of such a property.

\subsubsection{A real weighted site gap}

We first prove the flat block
inequality with its scale.
Let \(\bar\lambda\) be the
arithmetic mean on the
\(n^4\) sites of a block.
The exact variance identity is
\begin{equation}
 \sum_x|\lambda(x)-\bar\lambda|^2
       =\frac1{2n^4}\sum_{x,z}|\lambda(x)-\lambda(z)|^2 .
 \label{px:block-variance}
\end{equation}
Connect each pair by the
coordinate-order path.
Its length is at most
\(4n\). A fixed
oriented edge lies
in at most \(n^5\)
of these paths:
its two longitudinal
endpoint coordinates
give at most \(n^2\)
choices, and the
three other coordinates
give at most \(n^3\).
Cauchy on the path
and then \eqref{px:block-variance}
give a constant
times \(n^2\)
times the sum
of squared
edge differences.
Multiplying by
\(\eta^4\xi^{-2}\)
proves
\begin{equation}
 \xi^{-2}\|\lambda\|_{2,B}^2
  \le C\big\{
         \|\partial_{\rm int}\lambda\|_{2,B}^2
                              +\xi^2|\bar\lambda|^2\big\}.
 \label{px:flat-block-poincare}
\end{equation}
Here the fine norm uses
\(\eta^4\), and
\(\partial\) divides a
bond difference by
\(\eta\).
The mean part is
\(\eta^4n^4\xi^{-2}
|\bar\lambda|^2
=\xi^2|\bar\lambda|^2\).
For \(n=1\) the
variance vanishes
and the same
inequality holds.

Apply the real comb gauge
of \eqref{px:fine-comb-strip} in each pillar.
Only internal bonds are
used in the block
inequality, so the
gauges of neighboring
pillars may be
different. They
define a unitary
site gauge globally,
and all covariant
norms are unchanged.
In this frame
\begin{equation}
 \|(\partial_{\rm int}-D_{U,{\rm int}})\lambda\|_{2,B}
                       \le C_L\epsilon\,\xi^{-1}\|\lambda\|_{2,B}.
 \label{px:block-gradient-comparison}
\end{equation}
The estimate follows from
\(|\operatorname{Ad}(U_b)-1|
 \le C_L\epsilon\eta/\xi\)
and the at-most-eight
incidences at a site.

Let \(Q'_0\) be arithmetic
block average. \eqref{px:uniform-pillar-transport}, Cauchy for
the finite average
and \(\xi^4=n^4\eta^4\)
give
\begin{equation}
 \xi^4|(Q'_{\rm pill}-Q'_0)\lambda|^2
                        \le C_L\epsilon^2\|\lambda\|_{2,B}^2 .
 \label{px:block-average-comparison}
\end{equation}
Use \eqref{px:block-gradient-comparison}--\eqref{px:block-average-comparison} on
the right of \eqref{px:flat-block-poincare}.
The result is the
same two terms
with \(D_U\) and
\(Q'_{\rm pill}\),
plus
\(C_L\epsilon^2\xi^{-2}
\|\lambda\|_{2,B}^2\).
Choose the fixed
curvature ceiling
so that this
coefficient is
at most one half
of the left
coefficient.
Absorption proves
\begin{equation}
 \xi^{-2}\|\lambda\|_{2,B}^2
 \le C_L\big\{
       \|D_{U,{\rm int}}\lambda\|_{2,B}^2
                         +\xi^2|Q'_{\rm pill}\lambda|^2\big\}.
 \label{px:covariant-block-poincare}
\end{equation}

Sum over the disjoint pillars.
Every internal fine bond
is counted at most once;
all other gradient
terms in the full
energy are nonnegative.
Suppose
\(a(y)=c_y\xi_y^{-2}\)
with \(c_y\ge a_*>0\).
Then
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \sum_x\eta^4\xi(x)^{-2}|\lambda(x)|^2
 &\le C_{L,a_*}\big\{
        \|D_U\lambda\|_2^2
             +\langle Q'_{\rm pill}\lambda,
                              aQ'_{\rm pill}\lambda\rangle_{\rm tops}\big\}\\
 &=C_{L,a_*}\langle\lambda,L_{\rm site}\lambda\rangle .
 \end{split}
 \label{px:real-weighted-site-gap}
\end{equation}
This is the actual site
weighted gap, uniform
in depth, volume,
region shape and
real holonomy.
It uses the small
real curvature
and actual transport
construction; no
physical current
or criticality
is used.
Crossing-edge
energy is kept,
not replaced
by a clipped
block mean.

For a complex site vector
split into Hermitian
real and imaginary
parts. Since the
real unitary
connection is a
real matrix in
an orthonormal
Lie-algebra basis,
the same inequality
holds for its
Hermitian energy.
If the top scale
is at most one,
it in particular
gives an ordinary
finite \(L^2\)
gap independent
of the bare
mesh.
In other physical
units its smallest
unweighted gap
is scaled by
the inverse
square of the
largest local
scale.

\subsubsection{The complex site domain uses the actual iterated means}

The preceding transport argument has a
complex version with a fixed physical
radius, independent of the number
of fine sites. We give it to avoid
assuming a uniform radius for the
iterated site average.

Consider one step on a fixed
two-block neighborhood. Suppose
all its edge matrices satisfy
\(|W_b-1|\le a\), and let
\(\varpi=\sup|\partial W-1|\).
There are constants \(r_L,C_L\)
for which the actual means
and logarithms are admitted
if \(a,\varpi<r_L\), and
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 a_{\rm next}&\le La+C_La^2+C_L\varpi,\\
 \varpi_{\rm next}&\le
       L^2(1+C_La)\varpi+C_L\varpi^2 .
 \end{split}
 \label{px:complex-one-step-recurrences}
\end{equation}
For the first line, a central
straight product differs
from one by at most
\(La+C_La^2\).
Plaquette sliding bounds
each closed comparison
logarithm by \(C_L\varpi\):
all prefix transports
have condition number
at most \(1+C_La\)
on this finite
neighborhood.
The defining exponential
average therefore changes
the central product
by at most that
amount.

For the second line, take the
local complex comb gauge.
Its values and inverses
are \(1+O(C_La)\).
It sets the tree
bonds to one; each
remaining bond is
then \(1+O(C_L\varpi)\)
by the finite
plaquette sliding
identity.
In that gauge the
Taylor/flux argument
for the actual
one-step map gives
the coefficient
\(L^2\) and a
quadratic error
\(C_L\varpi^2\).
Conjugating the
fine and coarse
plaquettes through
the small complex
gauge changes their
norms by
\(1+C_La\).
This proves
\eqref{px:complex-one-step-recurrences}.
Complex covariance
here follows directly
from the conjugation
identity for the
small logarithm,
or from uniqueness
of the admitted
finite mean.
No absolute-value
formula is
continued
holomorphically.

These constants can be bounded
before an iteration is run.
The finite mean construction
has a joint raw-edge
holomorphic ball of radius
\(c/L\), with universal
supremum bounds; two scalar
Cauchy circles bound its
second derivative by
\(CL^2\).
A comb on the one-step
patch sweeps at most
\(CL^2\) plaquettes,
so its non-tree
logarithms have size
\(CL^2\varpi\).
The quadratic Taylor
error in the coarse
plaquette is therefore
at most
\(CL^2(L^2\varpi)^2
=CL^6\varpi^2\).
The fine logarithmic
curl error times
its \(L^2\) flux
factor has the
same upper order.
Prefix conjugations
cost \(1+CLa\).
For example
\(r_L=cL^{-3}\)
and \(C_L=CL^8\),
with fixed universal
shrinkages and
enlargements, suffice
in \eqref{px:complex-one-step-recurrences}.
This count uses
directional Cauchy
on the proved
full supremum
ball, not one
coordinate estimate
summed over all
field coordinates.

On a pillar let \(t_r=\xi_r/\xi\),
and normalize
\(A_r=a_r/t_r\),
\(V_r=\varpi_r/t_r^2\).
\eqref{px:complex-one-step-recurrences} implies,
with an increased fixed constant,
\begin{equation}
 Z_{r+1}\le Z_r+C_Lt_r(Z_r+Z_r^2),
            \qquad Z_r=A_r+V_r,\qquad
                 \sum_{r<j}t_r\le\frac1{L-1}.
 \label{px:complex-transport-gronwall}
\end{equation}
For \(Z_r\le1\), the factor
is at most \(1+2C_Lt_r\).
Its product is at most
\(\exp(2C_L/(L-1))\).
Choose \(Z_0\) below
one half the minimum
one-step chart radius
times the inverse
of this number.
Induction then gives
\(Z_r\le C_LZ_0\)
and keeps every step
in its chart.
The constants depend
on \(L\), not \(j\).
With the preceding finite
choices a sufficient
common small input
radius has the explicit
form
\(cL^{-3}\exp(-CL^8)\).
The precise numerical
constants are not
needed below, but
this gives a
positive lower
radius rather
than an asserted
upper cap.
The product of the
internal means and
its inverse have
norm at most
\(\exp(C_L\sum_ra_r)\).
Hence
\begin{equation}
 |\mathsf T_j(W;y,x)-1|\le C_LZ_0,\qquad
 |\mathsf T_j(W;y,x)|+
                  |\mathsf T_j(W;y,x)^{-1}|\le C_L .
 \label{px:complex-pillar-transport}
\end{equation}
This proves the existence
and boundedness of
the whole finite
hierarchical formula
on that domain.

Now start with a real field
satisfying \eqref{px:pillar-curvature}, put it
in the real comb gauge
\eqref{px:fine-comb-strip}, and let
\(W=e^{i\eta E}U\).
Assume the actual physical
first-order input satisfies
\begin{equation}
 h=\max\{\|\xi E\|_\infty,
                    \|\xi^2\nabla_UE\|_\infty\}\le h_L .
 \label{px:site-complex-input}
\end{equation}
In the comb frame the ordinary
first difference of \(E\)
differs from its covariant
one by
\(O(\epsilon\xi^{-1}|E|)\).
The elementary plaquette
product then gives
\(a_0\le C(\epsilon+h)\eta/\xi\)
and
\(\varpi_0\le
C(\epsilon+h+h^2)(\eta/\xi)^2\).
Thus the starting \(Z_0\)
in \eqref{px:complex-transport-gronwall} is at most
\(C(\epsilon+h)\).

Choose a fixed \(h_L>0\)
so that the same argument
holds with \(E\) replaced
by \(sE\) for
\(|s|<h_L/h\), and
assume \(h\le h_L/4\).
Reduce the real curvature
ceiling at the same
time so that
\(\epsilon\le h_L\)
and the resulting
starting \(Z_0\)
satisfies \eqref{px:complex-transport-gronwall}.
The transport is
holomorphic in \(s\)
on this disc, with
a uniform bound.
Cauchy's formula
on a smaller
concentric disc,
or the geometric
sum of its Taylor
coefficients, yields
\begin{equation}
 |\mathsf T_j(e^{i\eta E}U;y,x)
                       -\mathsf T_j(U;y,x)|\le C_Lh .
 \label{px:site-transport-lipschitz}
\end{equation}
The bound in \eqref{px:complex-pillar-transport} is
uniform in \(j\) and
in the number of
coordinates. This
is a single
directional Cauchy
argument on an
actual admitted
physical disc.
It does not
assert an
entrywise absolute
Hessian sum for
an arbitrary
many-variable
functional.

For the complex site average
write \(Q'_E\) and for
the real reference write
\(Q'_U\). The transported
finite-average calculation
used in \eqref{px:block-average-comparison} gives
\begin{equation}
 \|a^{1/2}(Q'_E-Q'_U)\lambda\|_{2,{\rm tops}}
                   \le C_Lh\,\|\xi^{-1}\lambda\|_2 .
 \label{px:complex-site-average-difference}
\end{equation}
Here the real row weights
satisfy
\(a(y)\le a^*\xi_y^{-2}\).
The proof squares the
average difference in
each disjoint pillar,
uses \eqref{px:site-transport-lipschitz}, and
sums its fine volume.
There is no factor
equal to the
number of
fine sites.
The same argument
applies to the
outer endpoint
extension \eqref{px:outward-site-extension}:
its neighborhood
uses one adjacent
scale, so the
input constants
change by fixed
powers of \(L\).

\subsubsection{Relative forms give the complex site inverse}

It remains to compare the actual
site operators, not their
unscaled matrix coefficients.
Let \(L_U\) be the real
site operator and let
\(L_E=D_{e^{i\eta E}U}^\sharp
D_{e^{i\eta E}U}+Q_E'^\sharp aQ'_E\).
The transposes in \(L_E\)
are bilinear analytic
transposes. At a real
reference they are
the usual Hermitian
adjoints.

For a fine bond the difference
of the two site derivatives
is bounded by
\(C|E_b||\lambda(b_+)|\).
Adjacent pillar scales
differ by at most the
fixed factor \(L\);
the region gaps exclude
a bare bond jumping
over another layer.
The finite incidence
count therefore gives
\begin{equation}
 \|(D_{e^{i\eta E}U}-D_U)\lambda\|_2
                        \le C_Lh\|\xi^{-1}\lambda\|_2 .
 \label{px:complex-site-gradient-difference}
\end{equation}
Keeping derivatives on the
two arguments, expand
the kinetic difference.
Use \eqref{px:complex-site-gradient-difference}, then
\eqref{px:complex-site-average-difference} for the mass
difference, and finally
the real weighted
site gap in \eqref{px:real-weighted-site-gap}.
For arbitrary complex
vectors \(v,w\),
this gives
\begin{equation}
 |\langle v,(L_E-L_U)w\rangle_{\rm H}|
 \le C_Lh\,
      \langle v,L_Uv\rangle_{\rm H}^{1/2}
      \langle w,L_Uw\rangle_{\rm H}^{1/2}.
 \label{px:relative-complex-site-form}
\end{equation}
For example the quadratic mass
term is
\((Q'_E-Q'_U)^\sharp
a(Q'_E-Q'_U)\); the
two cross terms contain
only one difference.
On replacing the left
argument by its complex
conjugate, the same
absolute bounds apply
to the analytic
bilinear transpose.
No Hermitian
conjugation of
the complex
coefficients is
inserted into
their definition.

Let
\(B_E=L_U^{-1/2}(L_E-L_U)L_U^{-1/2}\).
\eqref{px:relative-complex-site-form} proves
\(\|B_E\|_{2\to2}\le C_Lh\).
For \(C_Lh\le1/2\)
one has
\begin{equation}
 G'_E=L_U^{-1/2}(1+B_E)^{-1}L_U^{-1/2},\qquad
 \operatorname{Re}\langle\lambda,L_E\lambda\rangle_{\rm H}
                  \ge\tfrac12\langle\lambda,L_U\lambda\rangle_{\rm H}.
 \label{px:complex-site-inverse}
\end{equation}
The inverse is holomorphic
on the whole admitted
physical ball.
It has the same
weighted coercivity,
up to a fixed
factor, uniformly
in depth and
volume.
This is a
relative-form
argument. The
unscaled operator
norm of a
coefficient
perturbation
need not be
bounded as
\(\eta\downarrow0\).

The proof establishes the site
inverse part of the
primitive package.
It has not yet
established the
site Gram inverse,
the fine vector
Green function,
or the layered
current precision.
Those require
their separate
row, readout
and gap
arguments.

\subsubsection{Exponential decay from the weighted site form}

Let \(V\) denote multiplication by
\(\xi(x)^{-2}\) on sites.
The real gap in \eqref{px:real-weighted-site-gap} is
\(L_U\ge cV\).
We prove a weighted inverse
bound before converting it
to pointwise regularity.
This avoids estimating a
bare kinetic operator
by its unscaled norm.

Let \(\psi\) be bounded and
one-Lipschitz for \eqref{px:layer-metric},
and let \(M_s=e^{s\psi}\)
on sites. Use the value
\(\psi(b_-)\) on an edge
and \(\psi(y)\) on a
top. Put
\begin{equation}
 D_s=M_s^{\rm edge}D_UM_s^{-1},\qquad
 Q'_s=M_s^{\rm top}Q'_UM_s^{-1}.
 \label{px:site-weighted-rows}
\end{equation}
On an edge the two endpoint
values of \(\psi\) differ by
at most \(C_L\eta/\xi_b\).
Inside a pillar their
difference from the
top value is at most
a fixed constant.
The difference from
the unweighted row
therefore satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \|(D_s-D_U)\lambda\|_2
  +\|a^{1/2}(Q'_s-Q'_U)\lambda\|_{2,{\rm tops}}
               \le C_L|s|\|V^{1/2}\lambda\|_2
 \label{px:site-weighted-row-difference}
\end{equation}
for \(|s|\le s_L\).
The edge estimate follows
from \(|e^{st}-1|\le
C|s||t|\) on the
stated bounded interval.
For the site row use
the same estimate
in its finite
transported average,
then Cauchy with
the actual pillar
volume. Its
constant is
independent of
\(\|\psi\|_\infty\).

The conjugated form has the
exact factorization
\begin{equation}
 M_sL_UM_s^{-1}
              =D_{-s}^\sharp D_s+(Q'_{-s})^\sharp aQ'_s .
 \label{px:conjugated-site-form}
\end{equation}
Expanding it and using
\eqref{px:site-weighted-row-difference}, \eqref{px:real-weighted-site-gap} proves
a relative form error
at most \(C_L|s|\).
With a complex field
perturbation in the
ball of \eqref{px:complex-site-inverse},
the same calculation
gives error
\(C_L(h+|s|)\)
relative to the
real \(L_U\).
Choose both small
enough for that
number to be
at most one half.
All these forms
are invertible.

For any such inverse \(\mathcal G_s\),
testing the equation
\(L_s\lambda=V^{1/2}f\)
against \(\lambda\)
gives
\begin{equation}
 \|V^{1/2}\mathcal G_sV^{1/2}\|_{2\to2}
                                        \le 2/c .
 \label{px:weighted-site-inverse}
\end{equation}
Indeed its real part is at
least \((c/2)\|V^{1/2}\lambda\|_2^2\),
whereas the right
pairing is at most
\(\|V^{1/2}\lambda\|_2\|f\|_2\).
This proof uses neither
a normal matrix nor
a pointwise positive
complex kernel.

Choose
\(\psi(x)=\min\{d(x,\Delta(z)),N\}\).
It is one-Lipschitz.
The diameter of a
pillar in \eqref{px:layer-metric}
is bounded, so
on \(\Delta(y)\)
its value is at
least \(d(y,z)-C\)
after \(N\) is
large enough.
\eqref{px:weighted-site-inverse}
then yields
\begin{equation}
 \|P_yG'_EP_z\|_{2\to2}
       \le C_L\xi_y\xi_z e^{-m d(y,z)}
 \label{px:site-cell-l2-decay}
\end{equation}
for a fixed \(m=m(L)>0\).
On a finite torus take
the periodic distance.
On the cover first
use bounded \(N\)
and then increase
it. The constants
are independent
of this truncation.

In particular the normalized
operator \(V^{1/2}G'_EV^{1/2}\)
has exponentially decaying
cell \(L^2\) entries.
Its two-sided cell
Schur norm follows
from \eqref{px:metric-ball-count}--\eqref{px:summability-rate}
when the separation
is chosen with
\begin{equation}
             \frac{8\log L}{\rho}<m/2 .
 \label{px:site-separation-choice}
\end{equation}
The rate \(m\) above depends
only on the fixed one-step
constants and the site
gap; it does not depend
on \(\rho\). Thus this
is a genuine order of
choice: increase the
separation after those
constants, or verify
that the already chosen
separation satisfies
this finite inequality.
It is not an appeal
to unspecified
polynomial volume
growth.

\subsubsection{A scalar subsolution estimate at the fine mesh}

We use a local estimate whose proof
also explains why a fine Coulomb
singularity causes no loss in
\eqref{px:site-cell-l2-decay}. On the infinite scalar
fine lattice in four dimensions,
let \(\mathcal L=-\Delta_\eta\).
The positive heat kernel gives
a positive Green kernel
\begin{equation}
 G_0(x)=\int_0^\infty p_t^\eta(x)\,dt,\qquad
 |G_0(x)|\le C(|x|+\eta)^{-2},\quad
 |\nabla G_0(x)|\le C(|x|+\eta)^{-3}.
 \label{px:scalar-massless-kernel}
\end{equation}
These inequalities follow by
integrating the mesh-uniform
heat kernel derivative
bounds. For example split
at \(t=|x|^2\), use
a polynomial off-diagonal
tail before the split,
and \(Ct^{-2}\), respectively
\(Ct^{-5/2}\), afterwards.
At \(|x|\le\eta\)
the bounds are the
corresponding lattice
scaling bounds.
Also \(\mathcal LG_0\)
is the normalized
lattice delta, by
integrating
\(-\partial_tp_t^\eta\).

Suppose \(w\ge0\) and
\(\mathcal Lw\le F_0\)
on a ball of radius
\(2r\), \(r\ge8\eta\).
Choose a nonnegative
cutoff \(\chi\),
equal to one on
the \(r\)-ball,
supported in the
\(2r\)-ball, with
its first two
differences bounded
by \(Cr^{-1}\),
\(Cr^{-2}\).
At the center
\(x\), summation
by parts gives
\begin{equation}
 w(x)=
       \langle\chi G_0(x-\cdot),\mathcal Lw\rangle
             -\langle[\mathcal L,\chi]G_0(x-\cdot),w\rangle .
 \label{px:subsolution-cutoff-identity}
\end{equation}
All sums use \(\eta^4\).
This identity follows by
moving \(\mathcal L\)
off \(w\) and using
\(\mathcal LG_0=\delta_x\).
There is no derivative
of \(w\) in its
last term.
Since the first
test is nonnegative,
its contribution
is at most
\(CF_0r^2\).
Indeed the lattice
sum of \(G_0\)
on that ball
is at most
\(Cr^2\), by
dyadic shells.

The commutator is supported
on the cutoff annulus.
Writing it as
\((\mathcal L\chi)G_0\)
plus products of
first differences
shows that its
absolute value is
at most \(Cr^{-4}\)
there, by \eqref{px:scalar-massless-kernel}.
Cauchy and the
annulus volume
therefore prove
\begin{equation}
 w(x)\le C\{r^{-2}\|w\|_{2,B_{2r}}+r^2F_0\}.
 \label{px:scalar-subsolution-estimate}
\end{equation}
If \(r/\eta\) is bounded,
the point-value estimate
\(|w(x)|\le\eta^{-2}\|w\|_2\)
gives the same inequality
with a changed constant.
Thus the local
estimate is
uniform at
coarse meshes
as well.

For a real unitary connection,
let \(\lambda\) be Lie-algebra
valued and put \(w=|\lambda|\).
For \(\lambda(x)\ne0\), pair
each term
\(\lambda(x)-\operatorname{Ad}(U_{x,x'})\lambda(x')\)
with \(\lambda(x)/|\lambda(x)|\).
Unitarity gives
\begin{equation}
 -\Delta_\eta|\lambda|(x)
       \le |D_U^\sharp D_U\lambda(x)|.
 \label{px:discrete-kato}
\end{equation}
At a zero value of \(\lambda\)
the left side is nonpositive,
so the same inequality
holds. This proves
the covariant scalar
subsolution inequality
without differentiating
a gauge.
It is used only
on a patch with
the full covariant
Laplacian stencil.
Bare boundary
cells will use
the point-value
fallback instead.

\subsubsection{Pointwise site Green bounds}

First take a real \(U\) and
\(\lambda=G'_Uf\).
At a site in pillar
\(\Delta(y)\), the
mass part of its
equation obeys
\begin{equation}
 |(Q_U'^\sharp aQ'_U\lambda)(x)|
                 \le C_L\xi_y^{-4}\|\lambda\|_{2,\Delta(y)} .
 \label{px:site-mass-pointwise}
\end{equation}
In fact it is the transported
vector \(a(y)Q'_U\lambda(y)\),
whose norm is at most
\(a^*\xi_y^{-2}|Q'_U\lambda(y)|\).
Cauchy in the average
gives the additional
\(\xi_y^{-2}\).

Take a local ball of radius
comparable to \(\xi_y\).
It meets a bounded
\(L\)-dependent number
of pillars, all with
scales in
\([\xi_y/L,L\xi_y]\).
The gaps exclude a
second intervening
layer in that
ball once
\(\rho>C_LL\).
Call the corresponding
whole-pillar neighborhood
\(\mathcal N(y)\).
Its cells are at
bounded \(d\)-distance
from \(y\).
Apply \eqref{px:scalar-subsolution-estimate}--\eqref{px:site-mass-pointwise}
on a lift of this
ball. This proves
\begin{equation}
 \|\lambda\|_{\infty,\Delta(y)}
   \le C_L\xi_y^{-2}
                 \sum_{w\in\mathcal N(y)}\|\lambda\|_{2,\Delta(w)}
         +C_L\xi_y^2\|f\|_{\infty,\mathcal N(y)} .
 \label{px:site-local-l2-to-infinity}
\end{equation}
Near a boundary of the action
region, every pillar lacking
this full patch is bare:
the nonbare regions have
the prescribed gap from
that boundary. The
single-cell fallback
in \eqref{px:scalar-subsolution-estimate} proves
\eqref{px:site-local-l2-to-infinity} there directly.
On a torus the local
ball is lifted to
the periodic cover.
Its fixed radius
can meet only a
fixed number of
copies of a cell,
since every period
contains at least
two top blocks.
This changes only
the constant.

If \(f\) is supported in
\(\Delta(z)\), use \eqref{px:site-cell-l2-decay}
and
\(\|f\|_{2,\Delta(z)}
 \le\xi_z^2\|f\|_\infty\)
on the right side.
The far contribution is
\(C\xi_z^3\xi_y^{-1}
e^{-m d(y,z)}\|f\|_\infty\).
The local forcing term
has \(d(y,z)\le C_L\).
\eqref{px:level-barrier} absorbs
the scale ratio:
\begin{equation}
 \|G'_Uf\|_{\infty,\Delta(y)}
       \le C_L\xi_y^2
                e^{-m_1d(y,z)}\|f\|_\infty,
 \qquad 0<m_1<m-\frac{3\log L}{\rho}.
 \label{px:site-pointwise-green}
\end{equation}
Choosing the separation large
enough leaves a positive
fixed \(m_1\).
This is a pointwise
estimate for a
bounded cell source.
It is not a
uniform bound
on the Green
kernel evaluated
at two individual
fine sites.

The actual equation also gives
\begin{equation}
 \|D_U^\sharp D_UG'_Uf\|_{\infty,\Delta(y)}
                  \le C_Le^{-m_1d(y,z)}\|f\|_\infty .
 \label{px:site-laplacian-green}
\end{equation}
Use \(D_U^\sharp D_U\lambda
=f-Q_U'^\sharp aQ'_U\lambda\),
and bound its mass term
by the supremum on its
same pillar. The
cell diameter in
the layer metric
is bounded.

\subsubsection{Site gradients and their complex continuation}

For differentiated pointwise bounds use
the actual local gauge clause of the
regular-pair class. On the required
patch around a cell it supplies
a unitary gauge with
\begin{equation}
 U=e^{i\eta A},\qquad
 \xi|A|+\xi^2|\nabla A|\le a_{\rm loc},
                         \qquad a_{\rm loc}\le a_L .
 \label{px:site-local-coefficient-class}
\end{equation}
The constant \(a_L\) is fixed small.
Near one interface the patch may
be described in the finer
adjacent scale; converting
to \(\xi\) changes these
bounds by fixed powers
of \(L\).
The region gaps and
the fixed patch collar
are chosen to include
no third layer.
This gauge clause is
an input defining
the regular-pair
class. Deriving it
for an actual
background from
weaker tests is
the separate
background
estimate.

In this local gauge the site
equation is a scalar
componentwise Laplace
equation with first-
and zeroth-order
errors. Expanding
the transported
differences gives
\begin{equation}
 |\Delta_\eta\lambda|
 \le |f-Q'^\sharp aQ'\lambda|
       +C_La_{\rm loc}
          \{\xi^{-1}|\nabla\lambda|
                                      +\xi^{-2}|\lambda|\}.
 \label{px:site-scalar-equation}
\end{equation}
Each difference of a
link exponential costs
\(\eta|\nabla A|\);
each undifferentiated
link error costs
\(\eta|A|\).
After division by
the two powers of
\(\eta\) in the
Laplacian the
terms have exactly
the displayed
dimensions.

Here is the interior absorption
that supplies the gradient.
On a slightly larger ball
of radius \(C\xi\), put
\(M=\|\lambda\|_\infty\)
and
\(F=\|f-Q'^\sharp aQ'\lambda\|_\infty\).
Let \(d_b\) be distance
of a fine edge to
the ball boundary
and take the finite
maximum of
\(d_b|\nabla\lambda(b)|\).
If \(d_b\) is only
a fixed multiple
of \(\eta\), the
point-value bound
on a difference
controls it by
\(CM\).
Otherwise apply the
scalar interior gradient
estimate to a ball
of radius \(d_b/4\)
around an edge
where this maximum
is approached.
Distances in that
smaller ball are
comparable to
\(d_b\). Its
gradient supremum
is therefore at
most the weighted
maximum divided
by \(c d_b\).
Using \eqref{px:site-scalar-equation}
in the scalar
estimate gives
\begin{equation}
 \sup_b d_b|\nabla\lambda(b)|
       \le C_L(M+\xi^2F)
                       +C_La_{\rm loc}
                           \sup_b d_b|\nabla\lambda(b)|.
 \label{px:site-gradient-absorption}
\end{equation}
Choose \(C_La_{\rm loc}\le1/2\).
Absorption, \eqref{px:site-pointwise-green}--\eqref{px:site-laplacian-green}
and the scalar interior
Hölder estimate then give,
for a bounded source
in \(\Delta(z)\),
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \|\nabla_UG'_Uf\|_{\infty,\Delta(y)}
       &\le C_L\xi_y e^{-\delta d(y,z)}\|f\|_\infty,\\
 [\nabla_UG'_Uf]_{\alpha,\Delta(y)}
       &\le C_{L,\alpha}\xi_y^{1-\alpha}
                           e^{-\delta d(y,z)}\|f\|_\infty,
                       \qquad 0<\alpha<1 .
 \end{split}
 \label{px:site-gradient-green}
\end{equation}
The Hölder comparison is made
in the assigned local frame,
or with its declared
transport to a common
base. The bounded
potential and pointwise
gradient give the
transported version.
The constant is not
asserted bounded as
\(\alpha\uparrow1\).
Cells with a bounded
number of fine sites
use the direct
difference bound;
near the action
boundary they
are bare, as
already noted.

These pointwise estimates continue
to the actual complex site
operator by a stronger
norm argument than a
pointwise matrix
coefficient estimate.
For a fixed source cell
\(z\), let
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \|\lambda\|_{\mathcal Y_z}
   &=\sup_y e^{\delta d(y,z)}
       \max\{\xi_y^{-2}\|\lambda\|_{\infty,\Delta(y)},
              \xi_y^{-1}\|\nabla_U\lambda\|_{\infty,\Delta(y)}\},\\
 \|f\|_{\mathcal F_z}
   &=\sup_y e^{\delta d(y,z)}\|f\|_{\infty,\Delta(y)} .
 \end{split}
 \label{px:site-profile-spaces}
\end{equation}
Use a rate \(\delta\) strictly
below the cell Green rate,
with its spare rate
larger than the
ball-growth rate
in \eqref{px:metric-ball-count}. Summing
the bounded-source
cell estimates
then proves
\(\|G'_U\|_{\mathcal F_z\to\mathcal Y_z}
\le C_L\), uniformly
in \(z\).

For the actual left perturbation
\(U_E=e^{i\eta E}U\), expand
the two covariant site
differences and the
two site averages.
The kinetic difference
has a coefficient
bounded by \(|E|\)
on a first difference
of \(\lambda\), and
a coefficient bounded
by
\(|\nabla_UE|+|E|^2\)
on \(\lambda\).
The mass difference
uses \eqref{px:site-transport-lipschitz}, has
size \(C_Lh\xi^{-2}\),
and reads only
the same pillar.
Hence
\begin{equation}
 \|(L_E-L_U)\lambda\|_{\mathcal F_z}
                         \le C_Lh\|\lambda\|_{\mathcal Y_z}.
 \label{px:strong-site-perturbation}
\end{equation}
No second difference of
\(\lambda\) occurs:
the difference of two
connections in a
site Laplacian is
lower order.
The first-order
input on \(E\)
is used here;
its supremum
alone would
not bound the
zeroth-order
coefficient.
The metric diameter
of a pillar is
bounded, so the
profile weight
passes through
the mass average
with a fixed
factor.

For \(h\) below the resulting
fixed threshold, the series
\begin{equation}
 G'_E=\sum_{n\ge0}
            [-G'_U(L_E-L_U)]^nG'_U
 \label{px:strong-site-neumann}
\end{equation}
converges from \(\mathcal F_z\)
to \(\mathcal Y_z\).
At finite volume it
coincides with the
inverse already
constructed in
\eqref{px:complex-site-inverse}, by
uniqueness.
It therefore proves
the complex versions
of the pointwise
potential and
gradient estimates.
The equation supplies
the complex covariant
Laplacian bound.
In the same real
local frame,
\(e^{i\eta E}e^{i\eta A}\)
has a physical
logarithm with
the first-order
bounds
\(C(a_{\rm loc}+h)\).
The scalar interior
estimate then
gives the complex
Hölder member
as well.

The argument establishes the
site estimates for bounded
cell sources. A mixed
gradient with a
divergence source
has a Calderón--Zygmund
singularity and
requires its
specified cancellation
or Hölder input.
No uniform bound
for that mixed
operator on all
bounded raw
sources has
been inferred.

\subsubsection{The site Gram inverse has its own lower-bound proof}

Invertibility of \(G'\) does not by
itself give a uniform inverse for
\(Q'G'^2Q'^\sharp\). We prove
that estimate using site
bump functions.
Let \(\Xi\) multiply a
top value by \(\xi_y\).

Choose a fixed smooth scalar
bump \(\chi_y\), supported
in the middle portion
of its pillar and equal
to one on a smaller
middle portion.
Its first two
differences are bounded
by \(C\xi_y^{-1}\)
and \(C\xi_y^{-2}\).
The arithmetic average
\(\beta_y=Q'_0\chi_y\)
has a positive
lower bound
independent of
the fine mesh:
count the grid
points in that
smaller cube.
The finitely
coarse cases
use the center
point.

Use the real local gauge
\eqref{px:site-local-coefficient-class} on a neighborhood
of the pillar and
its one-fine-cell
collar.
In this gauge
the initial open
bond bound is
\(C a_{\rm loc}\eta/\xi_y\).
The recurrence
\eqref{px:pillar-open-recurrence}, with
the same real
curvature bound,
therefore puts
the hierarchical
transports within
\(C_L(a_{\rm loc}+\epsilon)\)
of one.
Consequently the
three by three
matrix
\(m_y\psi=Q'_U(\chi_y\psi)\)
equals
\(\beta_y I+
O(C_L(a_{\rm loc}+\epsilon))\).
For the fixed
small class
ceiling it is
invertible with
uniform bound.

Define a site lift on that
pillar by
\(\chi_y m_y^{-1}\psi(y)\)
in the local gauge and
undo the gauge.
At the node use
its transformed
frame as well.
The resulting
operator \(E_{\rm sm}\)
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 Q'_UE_{\rm sm}=1,\qquad
 \|E_{\rm sm}\psi\|_2\le C_L\|\psi\|_{2,{\rm tops}},\qquad
 \|L_UE_{\rm sm}\psi\|_2
                         \le C_L\|\Xi^{-2}\psi\|_{2,{\rm tops}} .
 \label{px:site-smooth-lift}
\end{equation}
The first equality holds
pillar by pillar, since
the site averages have
disjoint supports.
For the last inequality,
the covariant Laplacian
of one bump is
bounded by
\(C_L\xi_y^{-2}|\psi(y)|\).
Expand it in the
local gauge: the
second cutoff
differences, the
connection times
first differences,
and the differentiated
connection all have
that bound by
\eqref{px:site-local-coefficient-class}.
Its mass term
is the transported
vector \(a(y)\psi(y)\)
on the same pillar.
The volume is
\(\xi_y^4\), giving
the last \(L^2\)
scale in \eqref{px:site-smooth-lift}.
One fine collar
of different bumps
has bounded overlap,
since each fine
site has a fixed
number of neighbors.
For a bare pillar,
take the single
site bump; its
Laplacian is
bounded by
\(C\eta^{-2}|\psi|\),
which is exactly
the same scale.
Thus no missing
local gauge at
the outer bare
boundary is used.

For a real top vector \(\psi\),
use \eqref{px:site-smooth-lift} with
\(\Xi^4\psi\) and
the equation
\(L_UG'_U=1\):
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \|\Xi^2\psi\|_{2,{\rm tops}}^2
   &=\langle(Q'_U)^\sharp\psi,
                         E_{\rm sm}\Xi^4\psi\rangle\\
   &=\langle G'_U(Q'_U)^\sharp\psi,
                           L_UE_{\rm sm}\Xi^4\psi\rangle\\
   &\le C_L\|G'_U(Q'_U)^\sharp\psi\|_2
                            \|\Xi^2\psi\|_{2,{\rm tops}} .
 \end{split}
 \label{px:site-gram-duality}
\end{equation}
Divide by the last node norm,
with the zero case immediate.
This proves the operator lower
bound
\begin{equation}
 Q'_UG_U'^2(Q'_U)^\sharp\ge c_L\Xi^4 .
 \label{px:site-gram-lower}
\end{equation}
The \(\Xi^4\) test in \eqref{px:site-gram-duality}
is essential. Testing only
with \(E_{\rm sm}\psi\)
would give a weaker
ratio of two norms
and would not prove
the stated weighted
lower bound at
different local
scales.

For the upper bound and
locality, set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F_U=G'_U(Q'_U)^\sharp\Xi^{-2},\qquad
 M_U=\Xi^{-2}Q'_UG_U'^2(Q'_U)^\sharp\Xi^{-2}
                                      =\mathcal F_U^\sharp\mathcal F_U .
 \label{px:normalized-site-gram}
\end{equation}
The site injection \((Q'_U)^\sharp\)
is an isometry between
node \(L^2\) and
its transported constant
pillar fields.
\eqref{px:site-cell-l2-decay}
therefore bounds the
normalized cell entry
of \(\mathcal F_U\)
by
\begin{equation}
          C_L(\xi_y/\xi_z)e^{-m d(y,z)} .
 \label{px:site-column-cell-bound}
\end{equation}
The same estimate holds
for the complex
\(\mathcal F_E\), with
the bounded transport
condition numbers
already proved.
The cell summability
calculation with
\(p=1\) gives a
uniform exponential
two-sided Schur
norm of these
operators, after
increasing the
fixed separation
if needed.
Their products
therefore have
the same type
of norm.
In particular
\(c_LI\le M_U\le C_LI\)
at a real pair.

The complex perturbation is
uniform as well.
The finite matrix
\(\mathcal F_E\) is
holomorphic on the
actual physical
first-order ball
constructed above.
Its operator norm
is uniformly bounded
there by \eqref{px:site-column-cell-bound}.
Apply one scalar
Cauchy circle to
the line through
\(E\). This gives
\(\|\mathcal F_E-\mathcal F_U\|
\le C_Lh\),
independent of
the number of
coordinates.
Hence
\begin{equation}
 \|M_E-M_U\|_{2\to2}\le C_Lh,\qquad
                         \|M_E^{-1}\|_{2\to2}\le 2/c_L
 \label{px:complex-site-gram}
\end{equation}
on a fixed smaller ball.
Here \(M_E=\mathcal F_E^\sharp\mathcal F_E\)
uses the analytic
bilinear transpose.
Its norm difference
is bounded by
\((\|\mathcal F_E\|+\|\mathcal F_U\|)
\|\mathcal F_E-\mathcal F_U\|\).
The transpose has
the same Hilbert
operator norm in
the real weighted
orthonormal bases.
No Hermitian
positivity of
the complex
Gram matrix is
assumed.

An exponentially weighted
Schur norm also controls
its conjugation. For
a bounded node function
\(\psi\) that is one-Lipschitz
in \(d\), its cell
entries change by
the factor
\(e^{s(\psi(y)-\psi(z))}-1\).
The inequality
\begin{equation}
 |e^{st}-1|\le |s|\,|t|e^{|s||t|}
 \label{px:nonlocal-conjugation}
\end{equation}
and a spare fraction of
the exponential rate
bound this perturbation
by \(C_L|s|\) in
operator norm.
Indeed
\(\sup_{r\ge0}r e^{-\delta r/2}<\infty\).
Choose \(s\) small
and use \eqref{px:complex-site-gram}.
The inverse of the
conjugated \(M_E\)
is uniformly bounded.
The distance-weight
argument used for
\eqref{px:site-cell-l2-decay} gives
exponential entries
of \(M_E^{-1}\).

In the physical top pairing
the weighted orthonormal
basis at \(y\) is
\(\xi_y^{-2}\) times
the color basis.
If \(B_{yz}\) are
the entries of
\(M_E^{-1}\) in
those orthonormal
coordinates, then
\(\|B_{yz}\|\le C_Le^{-m_2d(y,z)}\).
Undoing both
\(\Xi^{-2}\)
factors and
the orthonormal
bases gives the
counting kernel
\begin{equation}
 \left|
 (Q'_EG_E'^2(Q'_E)^\sharp)^{-1}(y,z)
 \right|
                   \le C_L\xi_y^{-4}e^{-m_2d(y,z)} .
 \label{px:site-gram-counting-kernel}
\end{equation}
Explicitly the unnormalized
entries of \(M_E^{-1}\)
are
\((\xi_z^2/\xi_y^2)B_{yz}\).
Multiplying on the
left and right
by \(\xi_y^{-2}\),
\(\xi_z^{-2}\)
leaves \(\xi_y^{-4}B_{yz}\).
This explains the
asymmetric fourth
power in a
counting-kernel
formula, despite
symmetry in the
physical weighted
pairing.

Finally the actual site projector
has the representation
\begin{equation}
 R_E=1-\mathcal F_EM_E^{-1}\mathcal F_E^\sharp .
 \label{px:site-projector-kernel}
\end{equation}
It agrees with its original
Gram formula by \eqref{px:normalized-site-gram}.
The smoothing part has
an exponential cell
\(L^2\) Schur norm,
and the matrix is
holomorphic on the
whole smaller
physical ball.
At a real field
it is the orthogonal
projector already
identified.
This completes the
site Gram and
projector part
of the package.
Fine vector
coercivity,
mixed derivative
source norms
and the current
constraint terms
are not consequences
of \eqref{px:site-projector-kernel}.

\subsubsection{The physical fine-to-coarse readout is a Hessian identity}

We next identify the
three quadratic forms
in the physical
calculation.
This is a finite-dimensional
identity on any
admitted chart;
it precedes a
uniform inverse
estimate.
Let \(U\) be
the reference
critical field,
\(j_U\) its action
current, \(Q\)
the derivative
of the actual
straightened
constraint, and
\(\omega\) its
multiplier.
Take a fixed
reference slice,
so that its
linear condition
is \(RD_U^\sharp a=0\).

Criticality on that slice
already gives the full
stationarity equation
\begin{equation}
                         j_U=Q^\sharp\omega .
 \label{px:physical-stationarity}
\end{equation}
To see this, first note
that \(Q\mathsf S=Q\),
\(\mathsf S a\) is
in the slice, and
\(a-\mathsf S a=D_UG'RD_U^\sharp a\).
For \(a\in\ker Q\),
criticality annihilates
\(\mathsf Sa\);
the Ward identity
annihilates its
remaining gauge
part.
Thus \(j_U\)
annihilates
\(\ker Q\).
The finite-dimensional
annihilator identity
gives \eqref{px:physical-stationarity}.
When the row
space is the
actual independent
datum space,
\(Q\) is onto
and \(\omega\)
is unique.
Equivalently it
is unique whenever
the row Gram
inverse used in
\eqref{px:explicit-current-lift} exists.

Because \(Q\widehat H=1\),
\eqref{px:physical-stationarity} implies
\(\widehat H^\sharp j_U=\omega\).
Define the actual
Lagrangian Hessian
\begin{equation}
             K_{\rm L}=\mathscr D_U-\Delta^{(2)}[\omega].
 \label{px:physical-lagrangian-hessian}
\end{equation}
The quadratic constraint
term here is the
second derivative
of the same
straightened
constraint as \(Q\),
with the same
per-length pairing.
It cannot be
replaced by
the quadratic
part of a
different row map.

For the explicitly chosen
Ward correction \eqref{px:symmetric-current-correction},
the physical second
variant is therefore
\begin{equation}
 \widehat G_1[j_U]^{-1}
    =\mathsf S^\sharp K_{\rm L}\mathsf S
                      +D_URD_U^\sharp+Q^\sharp aQ .
 \label{px:physical-full-form}
\end{equation}
Let \(W_1=Q\widehat G_1[j_U]Q^\sharp\)
and \(H_1=\widehat G_1[j_U]Q^\sharp W_1^{-1}\).
The physical version
of \eqref{px:off-current-slice-defect} gives
\(RD_U^\sharp H_1=0\).
Consequently
\(\mathsf SH_1=H_1\),
and direct multiplication
of \eqref{px:physical-full-form} gives
\begin{equation}
                   H_1^\sharp K_{\rm L}H_1=W_1^{-1}-a .
 \label{px:physical-row-readout}
\end{equation}
For example,
\(H_1^\sharp\widehat G_1^{-1}H_1=W_1^{-1}\),
the gauge contribution
is zero, and the
row mass contributes
\(a\), since \(QH_1=1\).
This proves all
signs in \eqref{px:physical-row-readout}.
It does not
prove the existence
of either inverse.

Let the actual local
critical branch be
parametrized by a
coarse variation \(B\),
with reduced datum \(b(B)\).
Its derivative \(h_B\)
at zero is taken
in the fixed
reference slice.
Differentiated
stationarity gives
the constrained
linear equations
for \(K_{\rm L}\),
with row value
\(Db(0)\dot B\).
They imply
\begin{equation}
        h_B=H_1Db(0),\qquad
 D^2\mathcal A_{\rm eff}(0)
      =Db(0)^\sharp(W_1^{-1}-a)Db(0)
                            +\langle\omega,D^2b(0)\rangle .
 \label{px:coarse-action-hessian}
\end{equation}
Here \(\mathcal A_{\rm eff}\)
is the action evaluated
on that branch.
For the first assertion,
the differentiated
equation tested against
slice vectors in
\(\ker Q\) says
\(\mathsf S^\sharp K_{\rm L}h_B\)
lies in the range
of \(Q^\sharp\).
Adding \(Q^\sharp aQh_B\)
and using \eqref{px:physical-full-form}
then solves the
row problem by
its defining inverse.
For the second,
differentiate the
value function
twice.
The second derivative
of the branch
contracts with
\(j_U=Q^\sharp\omega\);
differentiating
its constraint
replaces that
contraction by
\(\omega D^2b-
\omega D^2q[h_B,h_B]\).
The latter term
is exactly the
subtraction in
\(K_{\rm L}\).

\subsubsection{Which coarse coordinates remove the datum curvature}

The statement \(b(B)=B\)
has a specific coordinate
meaning. In the
present chart the
actual coarse group
field is
\begin{equation}
                             V(B)(c)=e^{i\xi_cB(c)}V_0(c).
 \label{px:left-coarse-chart}
\end{equation}
The fine straightened
row logarithm is
relative to the
same reference
\(V_0\).
On an interior
row the exact
node identity
then gives \(b(B)(c)=B(c)\).
It holds for
nontrivial \(V_0(c)\)
as well.
No assertion
about the absolute
logarithm of
\(V(B)(c)\)
is involved.

An outward row instead has
its prescribed factor
at the finer outer
endpoint.
In raw notation
its equation is
\begin{equation}
       e^{i\xi_cb(B)(c)}
           =e^{i\xi_cB(c)}\operatorname{Ad}_{V_0(c)}
                                      v_z(B_{\rm int}) .
 \label{px:outward-datum-factor}
\end{equation}
It can have both
linear and quadratic
datum corrections.
If only the
highest active
level is varied,
the lower-level
data \(B_{\rm int}\)
in this factor
are fixed to zero.
Then \(v_z(0)=1\)
and the factor
is constant.
More generally
the next-step
support mask
must be checked
against every
outward carrier.
Deep interior
rows give an
immediate instance;
a mask by itself
does not change
a logarithmic
coordinate.

For contrast, if an absolute
coordinate \(W_c=\log(V_0(c))/i\)
is used and the variable
is still a relative
increment \(D\), its
new absolute logarithm is
\(\log(e^{iD}e^{iW_c})/i\).
Its second derivative
in \(D\) generally
does not vanish.
\eqref{px:coarse-action-hessian}
then retains its
datum-curvature term.
This distinction is
independent of
the support mask.

Let \(\iota\) inject the actual
active next-step coarse
bond variables into
the row space.
When the literal
map in \eqref{px:left-coarse-chart}--\eqref{px:outward-datum-factor}
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 Db(0)\iota=\iota,\qquad
                     D^2b(0)[\iota\,\cdot,\iota\,\cdot]=0,
 \label{px:active-datum-flatness}
\end{equation}
its coarse action
precision on those
variables is
\(\iota^\sharp(W_1^{-1}-a)\iota\).
Its coarse current
is
\(\iota^\sharp H_1^\sharp j_U\).
The restriction
\(\iota^\sharp\)
and the physical
dual weights are
part of the
readout, even
when notation
suppresses them.

\subsubsection{The next curved fibre inserts a different multiplier}

At the next lattice,
write raw bond increments
as \(D\), so that
the group field is
\(e^{iD}V\).
The actual plain
constraint logarithm
is
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak q_V(D)
    =\log\!\left(M(e^{iD}V)M(V)^{-1}\right)/i .
 \label{px:next-raw-constraint}
\end{equation}
Its local pivot graph
has derivative
\(C_V\), and
the pivot injection
\(h_V\) satisfies
\(D\mathfrak q_V(0)h_V=1\).
Twice differentiating
the graph equation
gives
\begin{equation}
 D^2\Phi_V(0)[u,v]
                =-h_VD^2\mathfrak q_V(0)[C_Vu,C_Vv].
 \label{px:next-graph-second-derivative}
\end{equation}
This is the actual
pivot graph, not
a free extension
chosen after the
Hessian.

Let \(\widehat K\) and
\(\widehat J\) be the
coarse effective action
Hessian and gradient
in these raw
counting coordinates.
The chain rule on
that graph is
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 D^2(\mathcal A_{\rm eff}\circ\Phi_V)(0)[u,v]
   ={}&\langle C_Vu,\widehat K C_Vv\rangle\\
     &-\langle h_V^\sharp\widehat J,
                   D^2\mathfrak q_V(0)[C_Vu,C_Vv]\rangle .
 \end{split}
 \label{px:next-constrained-hessian}
\end{equation}
Thus the next constraint
multiplier is
\(h_V^\sharp\widehat J\).
It is not
\(\widehat J\)
on the new
row space unless
the notation
already includes
this \(h_V^\sharp\).
Define \(E_V^{(2)}[\widehat J]\)
by this last
contraction.
With the actual
soft gauge Hessian
\(\widehat K_{\rm GF}\),
the next free
precision is
\begin{equation}
             C_V^\sharp
                \bigl(\widehat K-E_V^{(2)}[\widehat J]
                                      +\widehat K_{\rm GF}\bigr)C_V .
 \label{px:complete-next-precision}
\end{equation}
A gauge term relative
to \(V\) and the
absolute contour
gauge have equal
values on an
axial physical
reference.
Off that locus
their Hessians
can differ, as
shown in the
domain section.
\eqref{px:complete-next-precision}
uses the actual
gauge definition
of the model
being considered.

For a uniform next-lattice
spacing \(\xi\),
the raw and physical
conversions are
\begin{equation}
       \widehat K=\xi^2 K_{\rm phys,count},\qquad
                              \widehat J=\xi^3J_{\rm phys}.
 \label{px:coarse-raw-duality}
\end{equation}
Indeed
\(\xi^4\sum B(KB)=
\xi^2\sum D(KD)\)
when \(D=\xi B\),
and
\(\xi^4\sum J_{\rm phys}B=
\sum \xi^3J_{\rm phys}D\).
At nonuniform row
lengths the corresponding
diagonal length
matrices must be
kept on both
sides; their
commutation is
not assumed.
The coupling
coefficients in
the original
action remain
inside \(K\)
and \(J\).

Combining \eqref{px:physical-row-readout}, \eqref{px:active-datum-flatness}
and \eqref{px:next-constrained-hessian} gives the
physical diagram:
fine Lagrangian
Hessian, coarse
value Hessian,
then next-fibre
Hessian.
Each arrow has
its own row map,
its own dual
current, and
its own gauge
term.
The physical
identity proves
none of those
three objects
interchangeable.

For completeness the chosen
off-current extension
has an exact
additional readout.
Put \(h=H_1[J]\),
\(r=RD_U^\sharp h\),
\(\delta J=J-j_U\),
and \(K[J]=\mathscr D_U-
\Delta^{(2)}[\widehat H[J]^\sharp J]\).
Using \eqref{px:physical-invariant-hessian} in
\eqref{px:second-current-variant} gives
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 (Q\widehat G_1[J]Q^\sharp)^{-1}-a
   ={}&h^\sharp\mathsf S^\sharp K[J]\mathsf Sh
         -h^\sharp\mathcal B_U[\delta J]h+r^\sharp r .
 \end{split}
 \label{px:off-current-row-readout}
\end{equation}
All pairings are
bilinear on the
complex domain.
On a real pair
the last term
is nonnegative;
it vanishes on
the physical
graph.
The middle term
is a current
defect and does
not disappear
from a Ward
property alone.
For a separately
named normal form,
the complete
projected difference
between \eqref{px:complete-next-precision}
and that form
must be identified,
including its
horizontal multiplier
and gauge terms.

\subsubsection{A flat Feynman comparison on all the layers}

There is a useful vector
estimate which does not
involve the Landau
projection or an
independent current.
It uses the actual
flat straightened
averages.
We prove it to
specify exactly
what is available
before those two
additional operations.

First take the full periodic
fine lattice as the
ambient graph.
Let \(a_\mu(x)\)
be a fine vector
one-form, with
physical \(L^2\)
measure \(\eta^4\).
For a positive
level-\(j\) row
of length
\(\xi_j=n\eta\),
\(n=L^j\), its
flat per-length
average is
\begin{equation}
 (Q_j^0a)_\mu(y)
    =n^{-5}\sum_{u\in\mathcal B_n}
                      \sum_{t=0}^{n-1}a_\mu(y+\eta u+\eta t e_\mu).
 \label{px:flat-field-average}
\end{equation}
Here \(\mathcal B_n\)
is the centered
set of \(n^4\)
fine block sites.
The formula is
the flat straightened
map, not the
plain path map.
At \(j=0\)
it is the
identity.
The coefficient
of each fine
bond is nonnegative,
the coefficients
sum to one,
and each is at
most \(n^{-4}\).
The last fact
follows because
at most \(n\)
pairs \((u_\mu,t)\)
give a fixed
longitudinal
position, while
the three other
coordinates are
fixed.

Its support lies in the
union of the two
endpoint blocks.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 |Q_j^0a(c)|\le
               C\xi_j^{-2}\|a_\mu\|_{2,\mathcal D_c} .
 \label{px:flat-row-ltwo}
\end{equation}
For example Cauchy
gives
\(\sum_b w_b^2\le n^{-4}\)
from \(\sum_bw_b=1\)
and \(w_b\le n^{-4}\);
converting counting
\(L^2\) to physical
\(L^2\) contributes
\(\eta^{-2}\).
Thus the resulting
coefficient is
\(\eta^{-2}n^{-2}=\xi_j^{-2}\).
This bound is
specific to this
flat row formula.

For a fine bond \(b\),
put \(\xi_b\) equal
to the larger of
its endpoint pillar
scales and define
\begin{equation}
 \|a\|_{\rm mass}^2
          =\sum_b\eta^4\xi_b^{-2}|a(b)|^2,\qquad
 \mathcal E_{\rm F}^0(a)
     =\|\partial a\|_2^2+
                  \sum_{c\in\Gamma}c_c\xi_c^2|Q^0a(c)|^2 ,
 \quad 0<c_*\le c_c\le c^* .
 \label{px:flat-feynman-energy}
\end{equation}
The component gradient
contains all fine
coordinate differences
on the ambient
torus. The second
term is exactly
the physical row
pairing with
\(a(c)=c_c\xi_c^{-2}\).
In particular it
has neither an
extra fine volume
factor nor an
unweighted counting
transpose.

For each nonbare top \(y\)
and each direction \(\mu\),
one of the adjacent
level-\(j\) rows
has \(y\) as
an endpoint and
is a determining
row. Indeed the
excluded higher
region is a
union of aligned
blocks of side
at least \(L\xi_j\).
Along that
coordinate line,
the excluded
block containing
an exterior
point has at
least \(L\ge3\)
level-\(j\) sites.
Both neighboring
sites cannot
belong to the
higher region.
Choose one that
does not.
If the other
endpoint is
outside \(\Omega_j\),
this is precisely
an outward row,
which is retained.
At the highest
level there is
no higher
region to
exclude.

Let \(m_{y,\mu}\) be the
arithmetic mean of
\(a_\mu\) on the
pillar enlarged by
one fine cell.
A rectangular
carrier containing
that enlarged
pillar and the
chosen row's
two endpoint
blocks has side
length at most
\(C\xi_j\).
For \(j\ge1\)
it lies inside
the ambient
fine graph by
the nesting
gap.
The ordinary
box Poincare
inequality,
proved by the
coordinate-path
count used for
\eqref{px:uniform-pillar-transport}, gives
\begin{equation}
 |Q_j^0a(c(y,\mu))-m_{y,\mu}|
           \le C\xi_j^{-1}\|\partial a_\mu\|_{2,\mathcal D_{y,\mu}} .
 \label{px:flat-row-mean-comparison}
\end{equation}
To verify this without
a pointwise trace
estimate, subtract
the carrier's
arithmetic mean.
Both functionals
annihilate that
constant in
their difference
and have \(L^2\)
norm at most
\(C\xi_j^{-2}\).
Poincare then
supplies one
factor \(\xi_j\).

A second use of Poincare
on the enlarged
pillar gives
\begin{equation}
 \xi_j^{-2}\|a\|_{2,\mathcal B_y^+}^2
       \le C\sum_\mu\|\partial a_\mu\|_{2,\mathcal D_{y,\mu}}^2
                    +C\xi_j^2\sum_\mu|Q_j^0a(c(y,\mu))|^2 .
 \label{px:flat-field-local-poincare}
\end{equation}
Every fine bond with
a nonbare endpoint
can be assigned
to a pillar of
its larger endpoint
scale and is
included in
that pillar's
enlargement.
If both endpoints
are bare, its
level-zero row
is the identity
and controls it
directly.

The overlap in the gradient
sum is uniform.
For a fixed level,
all carrier centers
are on its grid
and their diameters
are \(C\xi_j\),
so a fine point
belongs to a
fixed number
of them.
A carrier of
an outward
level-\(j\) row
is inside
\(\Omega_{j-1}\),
and its endpoint
blocks are
outside
\(\Omega_{j+1}\).
Its one-fine-cell
collar can enter
only an adjacent
level.
Thus a fixed
fine point
is counted at
only a fixed
number of levels,
not at every
level of the
sequence.
Each chosen row
has at most its
two endpoints
as selecting
tops.
Summing \eqref{px:flat-field-local-poincare}
therefore proves
\begin{equation}
                         \|a\|_{\rm mass}^2
                                    \le C_L\mathcal E_{\rm F}^0(a).
 \label{px:flat-feynman-gap}
\end{equation}
The constants are
independent of
depth, fine mesh,
volume and
the shapes of
the separated
regions.
Periodic carriers
which wrap are
lifted to their
rectangles; the
compatible torus
has at least
two top blocks,
so the multiplicity
of that lift
is bounded.

There is also the upper
row estimate
\begin{equation}
              \sum_{c\in\Gamma}\xi_c^2|Q^0a(c)|^2
                                      \le C_L\|a\|_{\rm mass}^2 .
 \label{px:flat-field-row-upper}
\end{equation}
Use \eqref{px:flat-row-ltwo} on
each row carrier.
All fine endpoint
scales there are
comparable to
\(\xi_c\), within
the fixed adjacent
scale factor.
The preceding
overlap count
then applies.
\eqref{px:flat-feynman-gap}
and \eqref{px:flat-field-row-upper}
are estimates
for the
flat component
Feynman form.

For a proper active region,
extend the sequence
by bare cells on
the ambient torus
and compress this
full positive
form by zero
extension of its
active bond
coordinates.
Its lower bound
survives exactly:
apply \eqref{px:flat-feynman-gap}
to the extended
vector.
This is the
Dirichlet compression
of the component
Laplacian.
An inner-plaquette
Maxwell Hessian
has a different
boundary form.
Nor has the
nonlocal subtraction
\(D_U(1-R)D_U^\sharp\)
been included.
Those comparisons
are separate
in the vector
precision problem.

\subsubsection{What small curvature does to the actual Wilson Hessian}

The Wilson part admits a
relative form estimate
without assuming a
matrix norm bound.
We derive it directly
from the plaquette
product.
Use
\(\langle X,Y\rangle_{\rm col}
=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(XY)\)
on Hermitian traceless
matrices.
For a plaquette
with oriented bonds
\(b_1,\ldots,b_4\),
put \(P=U(b_1)\cdots U(b_4)\)
and \(T_{r-1}=U(b_1)\cdots U(b_{r-1})\).
A left variation
\(e^{i\eta v(b)}U(b)\)
inserts
\(X_r=\eta\operatorname{Ad}(T_{r-1})v(b_r)\).
On reversed bonds
the variation is
\(v(\bar b)=-\operatorname{Ad}(U(b)^{-1})v(b)\),
as follows by
inverting the
group field.

The varied plaquette is
\(\prod_{r=1}^4e^{iX_r}P\).
At \(P=1\), the
trace of the
mixed second
derivative is
the trace of
the product of
the two sums
of insertions.
Cyclicity of
the trace
cancels their
commutators.
For general real
\(P\), subtract
that calculation
and use the
factor \(P-1\)
in every
remaining term.
Thus the
plaquette action
\(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}P\)
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 D^2\mathcal A_p(U)[v,w]
     &=\left\langle\sum_rX_r,\sum_rY_r\right\rangle_{\rm col}
                                      +\mathcal R_p(v,w),\\
 |\mathcal R_p(v,w)|
     &\le C\|P-1\|
           \left(\sum_r|X_r|^2\right)^{1/2}
           \left(\sum_r|Y_r|^2\right)^{1/2}.
 \end{split}
 \label{px:plaquette-hessian-exact}
\end{equation}
There are only sixteen
mixed insertion terms.
Unitarity of the
prefixes makes
\(\sum|X_r|^2=\eta^2\sum|v(b_r)|^2\).
The same polynomial
trace expression,
with no real-part
operation, is its
holomorphic continuation.

Define the plaquette
linearized curl by
\begin{equation}
 (\mathfrak d_Uv)(p)
          =\eta^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^4
                              \operatorname{Ad}(T_{r-1})v(b_r).
 \label{px:plaquette-linearized-curl}
\end{equation}
Then \(\sum_rX_r=\eta^2\mathfrak d_Uv(p)\).
If
\(\|P-1\|\le\epsilon\eta^2\xi_p^{-2}\),
with \(\xi_p\)
the largest
corner scale,
summing \eqref{px:plaquette-hessian-exact}
over the actual
plaquettes gives
\begin{equation}
 \left|\langle v,\mathscr D_Uw\rangle
                       -\langle\mathfrak d_Uv,\mathfrak d_Uw\rangle_2\right|
              \le C_L\epsilon\|v\|_{\rm mass}\|w\|_{\rm mass}.
 \label{px:wilson-form-remainder}
\end{equation}
Every bond is in
at most six
unoriented
plaquettes.
Each error has
the factor
\(\eta^2\epsilon\xi_p^{-2}\)
from \(P-1\)
and another
\(\eta^2\)
from the two
insertions.
Their product
is the physical
\(\eta^4\) measure
times the
natural inverse
scale squared.
There is no
loss \(\epsilon\eta^{-2}\)
in this form
estimate.

This curl is close to the
ordinary forward
covariant curl
\(\mathrm{d}_Uv=\nabla_{U,\mu}v_\nu-
\nabla_{U,\nu}v_\mu\).
For example on a
\(\mu\nu\) plaquette
the difference
of their numerator
sums is
\begin{equation}
 (1-\operatorname{Ad}P)
           \bigl(\operatorname{Ad}U_\nu(x)v_\mu(x+\eta e_\nu)
                                                    +v_\nu(x)\bigr).
 \label{px:curl-convention-difference}
\end{equation}
Direct multiplication of
the four prefixes
proves this
identity.
It gives
\(\|\mathfrak d_Uv-\mathrm{d}_Uv\|_2
\le C_L\epsilon\|v\|_{\rm mass}\),
since \(\eta\le\xi_p\).
In particular
\begin{equation}
 \langle v,\mathscr D_Uv\rangle
     \ge(1-C_L\epsilon)\|\mathrm{d}_Uv\|_2^2
                                     -C_L\epsilon\|v\|_{\rm mass}^2
 \label{px:wilson-lower-form}
\end{equation}
for a real field,
after decreasing
the fixed
curvature ceiling.
Positive bounded
plaquette weights
give the same
statement with
their lower and
upper bounds.
Signed layer
profiles or
additional current
subtractions
must be estimated
separately.

On the full periodic graph,
the covariant Hodge
calculation is also
explicit:
\begin{equation}
 \left|
   \|\mathrm{d}_Uv\|_2^2+\|D_U^\sharp v\|_2^2
                              -\sum_\mu\|\nabla_{U,\mu}v\|_2^2
 \right|
                          \le C_L\epsilon\|v\|_{\rm mass}^2 .
 \label{px:covariant-hodge-error}
\end{equation}
Expand both squares.
The diagonal terms
agree because each
covariant shift is
unitary.
For different
directions the
uncancelled terms
are commutators
of the two shifts,
or of a shift
and an inverse
shift.
Their coefficients
are conjugates
of \(\operatorname{Ad}P-1\).
The two difference
denominators
contribute
\(\eta^{-2}\);
the plaquette
bound leaves
\(C\epsilon\xi^{-2}\).
There are a
fixed number
of neighboring
terms at each
bond.
Adjacent scales
are comparable,
so Cauchy proves
\eqref{px:covariant-hodge-error}.
On a proper
inner graph
the summation
by parts has
additional
boundary terms.

The full Feynman gauge
uses \(D_UD_U^\sharp\).
The actual fine
Landau form
instead uses
\(D_URD_U^\sharp\).
Its difference
is the nonnegative
real smoothing
form
\begin{equation}
          D_U(1-R)D_U^\sharp
             =(D_U\mathcal F_U)M_U^{-1}
                                      (D_U\mathcal F_U)^\sharp .
 \label{px:landau-feynman-difference}
\end{equation}
A lower bound for
the Feynman form
does not survive
this subtraction
by monotonicity.
This is one
reason the
vector coercivity
step remains
distinct from
the site gap
and \eqref{px:flat-feynman-gap}.

For the admitted complex
perturbation \(E\),
the actual plaquette
Taylor formula gives
\(\|P(U_E)-P(U)\|\le C_Lh\eta^2\xi_p^{-2}\).
Indeed the first
order boundary
sum of \(E\)
is its covariant
curl; the remaining
terms contain
either two
increments or
one increment
times a real
connection on
a local gauge
patch.
The first-order
core bounds
control each
by that scale.
Also
\(\|\mathrm{d}_{U_E}v-\mathrm{d}_Uv\|_2
\le C_Lh\|v\|_{\rm mass}\).
Subtracting \eqref{px:plaquette-hessian-exact}
therefore proves
\begin{equation}
 |\langle v,(\mathscr D_{U_E}-\mathscr D_U)w\rangle|
   \le C_Lh
       (\|\mathrm{d}_Uv\|_2+\|v\|_{\rm mass})
       (\|\mathrm{d}_Uw\|_2+\|w\|_{\rm mass}) .
 \label{px:complex-wilson-relative-form}
\end{equation}
This uses a physical
first-order
perturbation
radius, not
an unscaled
matrix norm
for the fine
precision.
It is a genuine
part of the
complex comparison.
The corresponding
actual field-row,
projected-current
and constraint
form comparisons
remain to be
joined to it.

\subsubsection{A mixed derivative needs cancellation}

One cannot replace those
comparisons by a
universal supremum
bound for every
order-zero
projection.
Already at a
flat field the
operator
\(\partial_1\partial_2(-\Delta+1)^{-1}\)
is not bounded
on \(L^\infty\).
Its kernel near
zero is
\(c\,x_1x_2|x|^{-6}\)
plus a locally
integrable term
in four
dimensions.
Let \(f_\eta\)
equal the sign
of this leading
kernel on the
annulus
\(C\eta<|x|<1/4\),
with a bounded
smooth cutoff
at its edges.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \|f_\eta\|_\infty\le1,\qquad
 \left|(\partial_1\partial_2(-\Delta+1)^{-1}f_\eta)(0)\right|
                                      \ge c\log(\eta^{-1})-C .
 \label{px:mixed-derivative-counterexample}
\end{equation}
The radial integral
is \(\int_{C\eta}^{1/4}dr/r\);
the angular integral
of \(|x_1x_2|/|x|^2\)
is positive.
The integrable
remainder is
uniformly bounded.
Discrete kernels
have the same
annular estimate
away from a
fixed number
of fine cells,
or the continuum
example follows
as a limit
of any proposed
uniform lattice
supremum estimate.

The required replacement has
a precise cancellation
form.
If a kernel \(K(x,z)\)
has size
\(C|x-z|^{-4}\)
on a cell of
scale \(\xi\),
and a uniformly
bounded constant-source
response, write
its action as
\begin{equation}
 \int K(x,z)(f(z)-f(x))\,dz
                  +f(x)\int K(x,z)\,dz .
 \label{px:holder-cancellation}
\end{equation}
For a transported
Hölder test,
the first term
is bounded by
\begin{equation}
        C[f]_\alpha
                 \int_0^{C\xi}r^{\alpha-1}\,dr
                  \le (C_\alpha\xi^\alpha)[f]_\alpha .
 \label{px:holder-singular-integral}
\end{equation}
The same shell
calculation applies
to fine sums,
with the first
shell at \(\eta\);
the bound remains
uniform as its lower
endpoint decreases.
The second term
is the stated
constant-source
response.
Thus an actual
mixed-kernel
estimate plus
its cancellation
clause gives
the required
Hölder-to-supremum
bound.
Size alone
does not.

For the fine gauge projection
\(\mathsf S=1-D_UG'RD_U^\sharp\),
this distinction is
material.
Its differentiated
site inverse
has order zero
at the fine
diagonal.
Energy estimates
use its \(L^2\)
form bounds;
point estimates
must either
keep it composed
with a smoothing
field Green
operator or
use actual
Hölder data
and \eqref{px:holder-cancellation}.
No unqualified
supremum Schur
norm of
\(\mathsf S\)
on arbitrary
bounded fine
fields is
being asserted.

\subsubsection{Compact dual bumps for the actual flat field rows}

We can also prove a uniform
right inverse for the
flat layered field
rows. This is a
different statement
from the site
lift \eqref{px:site-smooth-lift}.
The proof uses
two longitudinal
moments and a
strictly triangular
correction between
adjacent levels.

Fix a top \(y\) of
level \(j\ge1\),
put \(n=L^j=2m+1\),
and work on its
fine block
\(\eta\mathcal B_n+y\).
Choose a field
with just its
\(\mu\)-component
nonzero there:
\begin{equation}
 a_\mu(y+\eta u)
       =\psi\,\phi(u_\mu)
                         \prod_{\nu\ne\mu}\chi(u_\nu).
 \label{px:row-dual-bump}
\end{equation}
It is zero outside
the block and
on bonds whose
other endpoint
is outside.
For sufficiently
large \(n\),
take \(\chi(u)\)
from a fixed
even smooth
profile of
\(u/n\),
supported in
\((-1/4,1/4)\)
and positive
on a smaller
interval.
Write
\begin{equation}
 \beta=n^{-1}\sum_u\chi(u),\qquad
       \sigma=n^{-1}\sum_u(u/n)^2\chi(u).
 \label{px:row-profile-moments}
\end{equation}
Both have positive
lower and finite
upper bounds
independent of
\(n\).

For a fine longitudinal
position \(u\) in
this block, the
right coarse row
in \eqref{px:flat-field-average} counts
that bond
\(u+m+1\) times.
The left row
counts it
\(m-u\) times.
No other coarse
row sees it.
After the transverse
sums, their
two response
functionals are
\begin{equation}
 \ell_+(\phi)=\beta^3n^{-2}\sum_u(u+m+1)\phi(u),
 \qquad
 \ell_-(\phi)=\beta^3n^{-2}\sum_u(m-u)\phi(u).
 \label{px:two-row-moments}
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \phi_+(u)&=\beta^{-4}\chi(u)
           +\frac{m}{n}\frac{\beta^{-3}}{\sigma}
                                             \frac{u}{n}\chi(u),\\
 \phi_-(u)&=\beta^{-4}\chi(u)
           -\frac{m+1}{n}\frac{\beta^{-3}}{\sigma}
                                             \frac{u}{n}\chi(u).
 \end{split}
 \label{px:explicit-dual-profiles}
\end{equation}
Evenness gives
\(\sum u\chi(u)=0\).
Substitution into
\eqref{px:two-row-moments} now gives
\begin{equation}
 (\ell_+(\phi_+),\ell_-(\phi_+))=(1,0),\qquad
       (\ell_+(\phi_-),\ell_-(\phi_-))=(0,1).
 \label{px:dual-profile-exactness}
\end{equation}
For example the sum of
the two functionals
is \(\beta^3n^{-1}\sum\phi\).
For either profile
this is one;
the odd term
in \(\phi_+\)
sets the left
functional to
zero. The
right one is
then one.
The calculation
for \(\phi_-\)
is the same
with the other
moment.
The signed
profiles are
uniformly bounded
and their first
differences are
\(O(n^{-1})\).

The finitely many odd
values below this
smooth-profile range
need no limiting
argument.
Put the three
transverse profiles
at their center
point and use
longitudinal bonds
with positions
\(-1,0\).
Both endpoints
of these bonds
are in the
block for
\(n\ge3\).
Their two response
columns form
\begin{equation}
             n^{-5}
                    \begin{pmatrix}m&m+1\\m+1&m\end{pmatrix}.
 \label{px:finite-row-profile-matrix}
\end{equation}
Its determinant is
\(-n^{-9}\).
Its inverse
therefore gives
the required
two exact dual
profiles, with
a bound depending
only on the
fixed cutoff
between this
finite set
and the smooth
range.
That is a
universal constant,
not a depth
dependence.
